content: The windsock pattern or windsock lesion is a diagnostic indicator associated with left ventricular outflow tract aneurysms. Echocardiography Observations: 1. The windsock pattern is observed as a protrusion from the mitral valve into the left atrium and extending into the left ventricular outflow tract. 2. This pattern is visualized through echocardiographic imaging, which provides detailed views of the mitral valve and its relationship to the left atrium and left ventricular outflow tract. Pathomorphological Findings: 1. A gross anatomical image of a sinus of Valsalva aneurysm reveals a characteristic windsock-like opening beneath the anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve, extending into the right ventricle. 2. Another gross image shows a cross-section of the sinus of Valsalva aneurysm, providing a clear view of its internal structure. 3. Infected aneurysms of the sinus of Valsalva are documented, including cases with ruptured aortic cusps caused by endocarditis. 4. Some images depict aneurysms that are challenging to orient but still demonstrate the pathological features of the sinus of Valsalva aneurysm. 5. Infected sinus of Valsalva aneurysms are shown with natural coloration, highlighting extensive ulceration and fibrinous material due to Staphylococcus infection in a bicuspid valve. 6. Another infected aneurysm image shows fibrin exudate and valve scarring, though the aneurysm itself is not immediately visible. Careful examination reveals lesions caused by Staphylococcus infection. 7. 8. A hemorrhagic lesion in the left coronary sinus is observed in a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm, as seen in the left ventricular outflow tract. 9. A close-up view of a ruptured aneurysm in the aortic valve is provided, showing the natural coloration of the tissue. 10. Fixed tissue specimens of the sinus of Valsalva aneurysm demonstrate the aneurysm in the non-coronary cusp, with some images including a probe for better visualization. 11. Another fixed tissue image shows a close-up of the non-coronary sinus aneurysm with a probe, while a separate image provides a view without the probe. 12. A ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm is shown in a fixed tissue specimen, highlighting the rupture site below the tricuspid ring and the presence of a patent foramen ovale. Additional Resources: Numerous studies and case reports provide further insights into the diagnosis, pathology, and management of sinus of Valsalva aneurysms. These include: Fatal intrapericardial rupture cases. Pathological anatomy of aortic root deficiencies. Surgical repair techniques for ruptured aneurysms, including cases associated with Marfan syndrome and Behçet's disease. Rare cases of rupture due to fungal endocarditis or bacterial endocarditis. Imaging modalities such as echocardiography and magnetic resonance imaging for diagnosis. Long-term outcomes of surgical repair and classification systems for congenital aneurysms of the sinus of Valsalva. These findings and resources collectively enhance the understanding of the windsock pattern and sinus of Valsalva aneurysms, aiding in accurate diagnosis and effective treatment planning.
